items.stem: Which of the following best describes "TCP"?
options: A connection-oriented transport protocol that provides reliable, ordered delivery using sequence numbers, acknowledgements and retransmission
The process of choosing paths across interconnected networks along which packets are forwarded
An IP address assigned automatically for a limited time, normally by a DHCP server
The process in which each layer adds its own header (and sometimes trailer) to the data passed down from the layer above
items.answer: A connection-oriented transport protocol that provides reliable, ordered delivery using sequence numbers, acknowledgements and retransmission
items.markingKey: A. "TCP" is a connection-oriented transport protocol that provides reliable, ordered delivery using sequence numbers, acknowledgements and retransmission.

items.stem: A student claims: "Each layer of the TCP/IP model removes the headers of the layer above when sending." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: When sending, each layer adds its own header (encapsulation); headers are removed on receipt (de-encapsulation).
items.markingKey: When sending, each layer adds its own header (encapsulation); headers are removed on receipt (de-encapsulation). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:

Reason (R): DNS translates domain names into IP addresses.
Which option is correct?

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: A is false but R is true.
items.markingKey: D. A false (DNS is an application-layer protocol); R true.

items.stem: For each protocol, state the TCP/IP layer at which it operates and its purpose: DHCP, Wi-Fi (802.11), IMAP.
items.answer: DHCP – application layer, assigning IP addresses automatically; Wi-Fi (802.11) – link (network access) layer, sending frames over wireless LAN; IMAP – application layer, retrieving email while keeping it on the server
items.markingKey: 1 mark per protocol (layer and purpose): DHCP – application layer, assigning IP addresses automatically; Wi-Fi (802.11) – link (network access) layer, sending frames over wireless LAN; IMAP – application layer, retrieving email while keeping it on the server.

items.stem:

(b) Explain the difference between UDP and TCP. [2]
(c) A student claims: "HTTP is responsible for routing packets across the internet." Identify the error in this claim and correct it. [3]
items.answer: (a) A 16-bit number that identifies a specific application or service on a host, e.g. 443 for HTTPS (b) TCP is connection-oriented and reliable (handshake, acknowledgements, retransmission, ordering) but has more overhead; UDP is connectionless with no guarantees, so it is faster and lighter, suiting streaming and gaming. (c) HTTP is an application-layer protocol; routing is done by IP at the internet layer.

items.stem: An application sends 1000 bytes of data using TCP. The transport header is 20 bytes, the IP header 20 bytes and the Ethernet header plus trailer 18 bytes. Describe the encapsulation and calculate the frame size and the percentage of the frame that is application data.
items.answer: 1058 bytes; 94.5% data
items.markingKey: Data → TCP segment/datagram (+20) → IP packet (+20) → Ethernet frame (+18) (1-2 marks); total = 1000 + 20 + 20 + 18 = 1058 (A1); 1000/1058 = 94.5% (A1).

items.stem: A user in Singapore types https://www.example.org into a browser. Describe the protocols used at each layer of the TCP/IP model, from resolving the name to the page being displayed.
items.answer: Application: DNS query (UDP 53) resolves the name; HTTPS (HTTP over TLS) request on port 443. Transport: TCP three-way handshake, segments with sequence numbers and acknowledgements. Internet: IP packets with source and destination IP addresses routed hop by hop. Link: Ethernet/Wi-Fi frames with MAC addresses (ARP to find the gateway). Server responds; the browser renders HTML.
items.markingKey: Application: DNS query (UDP 53) resolves the name; HTTPS (HTTP over TLS) request on port 443. Transport: TCP three-way handshake, segments with sequence numbers and acknowledgements. Internet: IP packets with source and destination IP addresses routed hop by hop. Link: Ethernet/Wi-Fi frames with MAC addresses (ARP to find the gateway). Server responds; the browser renders HTML.

items.stem: "TCP should be used for all internet applications because it is reliable." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Reliability is not always the priority; real-time applications benefit from UDP-based protocols.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: guaranteed, ordered delivery; built-in congestion control. Arguments against: handshake and retransmission add latency; head-of-line blocking hurts real-time media; newer protocols (QUIC over UDP) achieve reliability with lower latency. Supported judgement: Reliability is not always the priority; real-time applications benefit from UDP-based protocols. items.answer: Every byte must arrive correctly and in order; TCP uses sequence numbers, acknowledgements and retransmission to guarantee this, which matters more than the small extra delay.

items.stem: An ISP in Santiago has six routers with links of different costs. Explain how a link-state protocol builds routing tables, apply Dijkstra's algorithm conceptually, and discuss what happens when a link fails.
items.answer: Each router discovers neighbours and link costs, floods link-state advertisements so all routers share the same topology map, then runs Dijkstra from itself: start with cost 0, repeatedly choose the unvisited router with the smallest tentative cost and update its neighbours, producing a shortest-path tree; the first hop on each path goes into the routing table. On failure, adjacent routers flood updates and every router recomputes, converging on new routes.
items.markingKey: Each router discovers neighbours and link costs, floods link-state advertisements so all routers share the same topology map, then runs Dijkstra from itself: start with cost 0, repeatedly choose the unvisited router with the smallest tentative cost and update its neighbours, producing a shortest-path tree; the first hop on each path goes into the routing table. On failure, adjacent routers flood updates and every router recomputes, converging on new routes.

items.stem: A 2.4 MB image is sent across the internet in packets with a 1200-byte payload. Describe how the image is split, routed, checked for errors and reassembled, calculating the number of packets.
items.answer: 2 400 000 / 1200 = 2000 packets. Each packet gets a header with source/destination IP, sequence number, TTL and checksum; routers forward each independently using routing tables; the receiver checks checksums, discards corrupted packets and requests retransmission (TCP ARQ via missing acknowledgements); packets are reordered by sequence number and reassembled into the file.
